analysis.one_liner: Penalizes drug companies that file sham FDA petitions to delay cheaper generic drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or vote, dying when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company wants to sell a cheaper copy of a brand-name drug, brand-name makers can file petitions with the FDA that sometimes delay approval for months or years. This bill would require anyone filing such a petition to certify under oath-like standards that it is factually grounded and not filed simply to delay competition. Petitioners who filed false or delay-for-delay's-sake petitions could face civil fines up to $1 million, suspension or loss of their right to file petitions, and referral to the FTC, and the FDA would have to decide every petition within six months.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who would get access to cheaper generic drugs sooner, and generic drug makers who would no longer face open-ended FDA delays caused by petitions filed to stall competition.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every petition on a generic drug application to certify that it includes all relevant information, is well grounded in fact and law, is not filed for an improper purpose such as causing unnecessary delay of competition, and contains no false or fraudulent statements; the FDA must investigate petitions that appear to violate these standards.

Authorizes the FDA to impose civil penalties up to $1,000,000 plus attorney fees, suspend petition rights for up to 10 years, revoke them permanently, or dismiss the petition, and to refer violations to the Federal Trade Commission for further action.

Requires the FDA to take final action on such petitions within six months with no extensions allowed; a petition not decided in time is automatically denied, ending the open-ended waits petitions could create.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose petitions as a low-cost way to delay generic competitors and could face million-dollar fines for abusive filings.

drawbacks.text: The six-month deadline with no extensions, even by petitioner consent, could force the FDA to rush decisions on complex safety questions, and petitions not decided in time would be automatically denied.

The same certification and penalty regime that targets abusive corporate filings could deter good-faith petitions from patient groups, doctors, or consumers raising genuine safety concerns, since penalties reach any knowingly false or improperly purposeful petition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks a real, documented frustration for consumers: petitions that can stall cheaper generics for long periods. Its core idea — certify the petition is honest and decide it on a firm clock — is a reasonable fix, but the blunt six-month no-extension rule and heavy penalties carry a genuine risk of chilling legitimate safety petitions. A better-designed version might distinguish abusive filings from sincere ones, but the bill's main effect would have been to speed generic competition and lower drug prices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Herb Kohl introduced the bill with Sen. Patrick Leahy as original cosponsor on January 4, 2007.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it expired with the 110th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept an unpenalized way to delay generic competition through FDA petitions, and consumers continued paying brand-name prices for longer. The committee's decision to never take up the bill preserved that status quo.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; the bill was introduced for Kohl and himself.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a markup or vote; it died in committee.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Industry sector affected by the bill
against.what_they_did: Had a direct financial interest in keeping petitions as an unpenalized delay tool; the bill targeted the practice of filing petitions to delay generic competition.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and the bill never reached a vote, so the record shows no party split to measure; it simply died in committee with one cosponsor.

industries.note: These companies use FDA petitions as a way to delay approval of cheaper generic competitors, and the bill would have made that expensive: fines up to $1 million, suspension or permanent loss of petition rights, and a mandatory six-month decision clock. Their gain from the bill dying is consumers' continued higher drug prices.
A six-month decision deadline would have cleared generic applications to market faster, expanding their business while cutting what patients pay.
